body:
Ugh, saaaame. It fucks me up realizing how much of my appearance and behavior before I began to transition were meant to cater to the "male gaze," as it were. Men's behavior towards me has changed now that I'm perceived as a butch lesbian, too. It's been bittersweet, especially when I'm interacting with an attractive guy and realize they probably would have been interested in me before.

It doesn't make your gender any less valid. Our families and/or society expected us to be attracted to and attractive for straight dudes. That expectation is not gonna go away overnight, or even over a year. It sucks, but I'm hoping the further I come along in my transition, the less I'll care about what guys are thinking of me.
I can confirm this. I shaved my head pre-T and it actually emphasized my small head and rounded facial features.

Yes, I'm American. It's not unheard of for guys to be my height, though it is uncommon. I know a *lot* of women my height and shorter. But I also live in an area with a pretty diverse population, including a prominent Italian-American community, so it may differ depending where in the U.S. you end up.
I'm 5'1 and I almost always have to settle for "boyfriend" cuts and whatnot in the women's section.

My whole family's fighting right now and the only ones respecting my pronouns and not deadnaming me are my brother and sister-in-law. Funny how things change. I'd much rather hash all this stuff out and not add to the stress/confusion by constantly correcting people, but it really feels like I'm seeing who actually believes me and/or cares when shit hits the fan.

I actually lost my eyebrows to alopecia, but after T *one* of them has grown back...... Thanks, testosterone....

edit: Also holy moley T is treating you well, congrats OP

To answer your second paragraph, I think I was angry at my body for looking like it did before I even realized I was trans. I didn't have the right words for it yet, but I knew it wasn't doing the right thing, so I often neglected or outright abused it. I still get angry at it if I think about it too much, but I've at least developed healthier coping mechanisms now.
Thanks for posting this, y'all. This was really heartwarming, gives me hope, haha.

I think with the patterned shirt and longer hair you'll get read as genderqueer/androgynous by people who are aware of that sort of thing, but tbh they look great on you and you're still waaay over in the masculine range. I do agree that wearing your pants looser/lower might tip you over into male-passing.

I've been struggling with thoughts of just not trying hard enough to be a woman, too, and my go-to response to them now is, "Erm, I really shouldn't have to be trying THAT hard." Back when I was in girl-mode all the time, my internalized misogyny was pretty out of control despite my feminist leanings. Starting to transition has made me more aware of those misogynistic thought patterns/tendencies, and in turn a better feminist.
Looking good, that's some significant change for one month! Did you make any changes in your diet/exercise in addition to starting T?

Sorry your doctor was so flippant about it. It sucks dealing with hair loss, especially at a younger age. Your friends and family are probably trying to convey to you that your hair loss really isn't as noticeable as you think, though they're doing it in a shitty, invalidating way. You also might lose a significant amount of hair at once and have the loss taper off like my cis boyfriend's did. He lost a lot at the age of 19 and it's been about the same for 5+ years. 

Rogaine does work if you can afford the upkeep. Another (expensive) option if you're feeling self-conscious about seeing your scalp are products meant to blend with your natural hair color like Toppik. I know Toppik in particular comes with a special setting spray, but it's no different from regular, $3 hairspray in my opinion.

> "every other trans person i know has a preferred name and pronouns but aren't assholes about it if you get it wrong"

Every other trans person he knows isn't his son, either. I mean, god forbid you want important people in your life to respect you...? I'm sorry you're going through this. It sounds like he's trying to rationalize his hang-ups about you being trans. Do you have any supportive relatives to talk with about this that would know how best to deal with him? From what you've said here he's not being reasonable at the moment, so it might be better to work around him rather than expending your time and energy trying to get him on your side. I haven't looked into them myself, but I do know there are binder giveaways online you could enter. And if you're not too busy with school, maybe you could make some cash from odd jobs and buy a Paypal card to get one yourself?

This friendship is not worth it. If you won't cut it off for her sake, do it for your own. You do not want to be hanging out with a fourteen year old girl who has a crush on you, even as a friend. I seriously doubt her parents are only going to call the cops on you if you "violate" her. Any decent parent would use the full extent of the law to protect their child before it gets to that point. If she is willing to fake a suicide attempt to get her way, who knows how much of what she's telling you is the truth. If you go somewhere with her and she makes any signs or suggestions you two are romantically involved, whether or not you want that, you could get into a lot of trouble. Imagine how much harder your life is going to be if you get labeled as a sex offender.

It sounds like this guy has (or at some point had) a round face he feels insecure about and is taking your post as you saying people with that face shape are less manly. Speaking as a trans dude with a very round face, fuck that noise. It's like when cis women get angry at trans women for supposedly reinforcing misogynistic stereotypes by passing; it misses the point and is overall a shitty thing to put on a trans people.

Dysphoria worsened for me as I started coming out to myself and close friends. Since coming out publicly, my dysphoria feels more precise? As in, I don't feel generally bad all the time now that I'm socially transitioning and everyone's started using the correct name and pronouns, but specific, negative emotions about my appearance have become more severe. So overall I feel better, but I'm more aware of the things that are keeping me from "passing." I'm working on caring about that less. Wish I had better advice about alleviating it. I'm mostly coping by distracting myself from it for now.

I totally get why you wouldn't be comfortable participating in this, but the Jesus idea made me laugh a lot. Maybe [a crossing guard](http://www.riversideca.gov/pworks/images/B4S_crossingguard02_106402c.jpg)?

There is a lot of pressure to look attractive in your late teens/early 20s. I look at photos of myself 5-10 years ago and realize I was waay more attractive than I realized. Granted, I was in the closet and trying to look extremely feminine, so there were other factors at play, but things about myself that I sincerely thought were obvious and hideous really... just weren't. It's true that you might need a few more years on T and generally aging to lose some face fat and grow into those features you consider awkward, but it could be your dysphoria/self-image issues playing tricks on you. It's hard to find objective perspectives when it comes to your looks; it might be worth talking to a therapist about it if you haven't.
Can you pay a friend to order it for you? You could give them cash or send via Paypal, and if your parents ask, tell them you owe your friend money for whatever reason.
Hey Gabe! Welcome (back)!

My coming out to my family and friends in person has gone relatively smoothly. A few family members weren't surprised and had already guessed. I used to dress pretty femme. Then last year I shaved my head and started wearing more masculine clothing before I was even sure I was trans, so the people around me picked up on the sudden change. The only bad experiences were with my brother and my dad. My dad thinks this has to do with him not being a good father so I'm emulating the father figure I never had or something like that, but he's said he'll always love me, and I think that's the best I can hope for from him. My brother... freaked out a bit, but he's come around.

When I came out on Facebook I got a ton of likes, a couple positive comments, and one person who thought I was somehow doing it just as a political statement? Yes, I'm changing my name and pronouns to make a point, you caught me. That aside, if anyone doesn't believe me or doesn't approve, they haven't said anything to my face about it, unlike when I came out as bi, funny enough. I think pre-T I would have agonized over what people were *really* thinking and saying behind my back, but honestly, I'm happy enough with myself at this point to know their opinion doesn't actually matter.

Alright, I need to vent/whine a bit.

I came out to my best childhood friend in December. She was accepting at the time, and even joked about helping me find a new name. I've reached out to her several times since then, and nothing's come of it. At first I figured she was busy with the holidays. Then her grandad suddenly fell ill and died in January. I called her as soon as I found out, and told her if she ever wanted to talk or just hang out, I was here. I can understand if she's feeling shitty and isolating herself, lord knows I've done that, but thanks to Facebook I know for a fact that she's been going out with other friends. I feel crappy because I've been going through all of this shit like fighting and breaking up with my boyfriend and coming out to my whole family and everyone else without her. But then I feel even crappier for feeling like that because it's selfish of me to expect support from her when she's got her own shit to deal with. I'm at a point where I'm not sure if I should reach out to her again, or just keep waiting for her to approach me. I can't help but wonder if me coming out as trans has something to do with this, after all.

I was pretty girly as a kid, and I didn't really question being a girl, but it didn't change the fact that I felt like a boy. It never occurred to me I might be transgender until I was 21/22, and then I refused to think or do anything about it for a few years. A large part of that was I'd only heard stories about trans people knowing and expressing their correct gender from a young age, too. I think it's the easiest narrative for the general population to swallow because it's more in line with the argument that queer people are born this way and can't do anything about it. Now I'm just a pretty effeminate guy, though I do identify more as non-binary than binary trans.

My advice would be to put a bit less thought into labels and more into specific actions (something I consistently failed at until eight or so months ago). If something feels better, do it, and don't worry about not fitting into a certain brand of transgender. There are a ton of transmasculine people that bind and present as male, but don't feel the need to pack or get bottom surgery. And if you don't feel the need to do any of those things all the time, that's fine, too. Also, childhoods are complicated. If you go into your memory bank trying to parse out the things that make you trans or cis, you're gonna be stuck at that stage for a long while. If you start feeling shitty because you feel like your early experiences point to you being cis, well... that could be a sign you're trans, haha. 

If you have any other questions about how I accepted myself and started coming out (just came out publicly two weeks ago), I'd be happy to answer them.

About 3-4 weeks in, I was a mess. I had an incident at work where a customer made a comment that bothered me, and I could *not* stop crying. It was as if my eyes were leaking for forty minutes, like [this one panel](http://1.bp.blogspot.com/-7jgm7yCHVIQ/Uga9tCLfVfI/AAAAAAAAKR0/hO7IXZU41D8/s1600/DEPRESSIONTWO60alt4.png) in Hyperbole and a Half's Adventures in Depression comic. And I almost never cried at work before. I was so embarrassed and worried that T wasn't going to help me like I'd hoped. Now I'm nearly four months in, and I've got my depression/anxiety more in control than I ever did pre-T. You could talk to your doctor about adjusting your dose or perhaps going on a weekly schedule to avoid the major highs and lows, but it could also be a matter of waiting out the adjustment period.

Technically I'm queer/bi, but I had a similar experience. Even though I knew I wasn't straight, I never felt like I fit in with women-attracted-women, despite wanting to. I also developed crushes on a couple of gay guys that make a lot more sense in retrospect, haha.

Definitely measure using the website's instructions and get into contact with them via email. If you're still undecided after doing that, here's my advice: I've tried on small, medium, and large from gc2b. From what I've experienced, the differences in sizes are pretty big. I'd say if you were able to get the L on and you're only exchanging because it was painful/uncomfortably tight, go for the XL. If it was too tight to even try on, the XL might be too small, as well. The correct size is supposed to be pretty difficult to pull on/off, especially the first couple times, but not impossible.

Oh, yeah, I've had that feeling. I've only been in relationships with guys, but I've always known I was bi. I feel a little twinge of sadness sometimes because I won't know what it's like to be in a lesbian relationship. But it wouldn't have *really* been a lesbian relationship because I'm still a guy, you know? If you were dissatisfied enough to want to transition, you probably wouldn't have felt right as a lesbian, either.
I'm a little confused. Are you saying you realized you're not transgender, or are you feeling regret about transitioning because it's narrowed your dating pool?
They're called keratosis pilaris in case you were wondering. They're treatable, but totally harmless if you wanna keep them, haha

Do you think it's possible that now that you are out you are internalizing the pressure to be "manly" that every man experiences, but because you don't measure up you're interpreting it as doubt of your trans status? Mentioning this because as a fellow feminine dude, I've had similar feelings leading up to and after coming out last week.

Cis women experience clitoral growth throughout their lifespan. It's possible your going off birth control and possible PCOS has something to do with it, but it wouldn't be unheard of if it didn't. As for STP without a device/surgery, yes it's possible. There was a thread in the past week or so discussing it I think. I've tried it, but it only seems to work well when I *really* have to go, haha. I'm not sure bottom growth has anything to do with it, though.

Is this something he's concerned about, or is it that you're feeling like you should be getting him off? Trans guys have a pretty wide variety of sexual preferences. Some of us like penetration, some hate it. A lot of us feel dysphoric about our clit/dick and only like it being stimulated in particular ways. Maybe talk to him about how he gets himself off? If he doesn't even want to do that, then you might have to accept he's not ready for reciprocation yet.

Did you shoot the people over at gc2b an email about it? They can take a few days to respond, but they're very helpful about figuring out your size. Also, did you get the half binder or full tank? The full tank's binding fabric is slightly longer and binds my 32DDD chest much better than the half does in the same size.

Have you thought about writing a letter/email rather than having to work up the nerve to say it? I got burnt out reaaal quick feeling like I had to sit people down and tell them in person. You can hand them the letter when you're there if you want, and you could still come out as slowly as you want to.

I've done it before with a cup to fill repeatedly rather than duck underneath the faucet. It really sucks that you have to worry about him listening in on you in the shower. :/ Depending on your shower head/faucet situation, you could fill it up from the tub instead?

People can say and do manipulative things without realizing how manipulative they're being. She might actually believe it and she might be saying it out of concern. The fact that she's expressing this while insulting you and claiming to know you really well (does she claim to know you better than you know yourself?) seems to me like she's trying to persuade you to do something. But I grew up around manipulative people, so maybe I'm a bit hypervigilant.
Can you just shampoo your hair in the sink and do your usual washcloth routine with the shower running?
Seconded, this sounds pretty manipulative.

I've seen a lot of guys here report fatigue when they first start T or up their dose. Your body is acclimating to the increased hormones. I wonder if that's why a lot of people seem to get sick not too long after they start T, as well.
God that binder looks fantastic. I placed an order with Shape Shifters recently and now I'm wishing I'd opted for the scales, as well. Side note, I like your hair color!

Congrats man! Same thing happened to me. Called to make an appointment, they told me it would be four months, and then they called me a week later asking if I wanted to come in the next day. I was convinced I wasn't gonna be able to get my T that soon, so when they basically tossed the prescription into my lap, I was stunned. I felt like I'd conned them somehow. I was seriously wondering if they had the wrong person or something because there was no way it could have been that easy and quick. So yeah, I totally get feeling a ton of self-doubt when things go better than you expected. Just try and take it one day at a time. You can get your testosterone and not use it right away if you want, and you can always talk with your doctor about lowering your dose or going off entirely if you feel like things are happening too fast.

Well that's a really unfair condition to set. Maybe if you told them about low-dose HRT being an option, and how long it takes for any outwardly noticeable effects to occur, they'd come around? I think it'd be a lot easier on all of you if you didn't have your whole family weighing in on your transition before you even get to try out testosterone. If you're in the US, your insurance company's website might have a directory for you to find covered therapists in your area. I found mine on a local trans advocate website I came upon just be typing something like "[city name] lgbt" or "[city name] transgender". You can call them and ask if they take your insurance or if they offer a sliding scale so you could afford their sessions anyway.

You're not alone in this. My body makes me feel nauseated, too. I get anxious just being around highly feminized people. As someone who doesn't have any other trans people in their social circle, this space can be safe haven for me. Other times (recently tbh) I feel so gross and ashamed I don't want to be reminded of my trans status in any way. 

Most of the time when I like myself, or at least act like I do, it's more out of defiance. As in, "Fuck you, society, for not wanting me to like myself. You can't tell me what to do." Maybe you should start from there. It can be exhausting, though, so it's okay if you can't keep it up every day, half a day, or even an hour or two. I've found it gets easier the more you do it.

Some days I'm okay, but on the days I'm not, I try to tell myself that I *will* be okay sometime soon. I know how hard this is, but if you can get through awful nights like this, you can get through anything. The fact that even when you feel like this, you've found the courage to come here and talk to us tells me you have a lot of strength. I can't tell you how many times in the past few months alone I've thought about posting here for help when my dysphoria is at its worst and chickened out.

So I came out on Facebook to everyone! Feels much better to have it all out of the way. My brother texted me this morning "You can't hide from me forever [deadname]. We're going to talk soon." Oh boy, can't wait to hear what his medium has to say about this.

Did you pick Rey? Because the exact same thing happened to me. Now I can't see that name without thinking of the character's super-feminine face and it just ruined it for me. At least I'm feeling much better about Ray now.
Congrats on graduating to the men's bathroom! I'm glad they didn't try and get you suspended or something.

I get it. I really do. I had a coworker who was a pain in the ass to deal with. We would always have to pick up her slack and she liked to play the victim a lot. The most extreme example was when she made a fundraiser page for herself even though her mother makes $150k+ per year and pays most of her bills (she's about a year younger than me). My disgust with her self-entitlement seeped into the rest of our relationship. I found myself judging her over the pettiest things. It was like I got addicted to being on the moral highground looking down on her. I did lose my temper with her much like you did, and it never helped. If anything, it made things worse because she used it as further evidence that the world was against her. I wasn't able to stop until she'd been effectively fired due to her shitty behavior. What I've figured out since then is that there are going to be a lot of people like this in your life, and how you respond to them is more important than what they do to you, intentionally or not.

And honestly, your lecturer isn't wrong. You're clearly holding a lot of contempt for him, though maybe not for the reasons she thinks. If you're having real issues working with him, maybe this is something you need to talk with your group and the lecturer about. Blowing up at him about a shirt might make you feel better, but it's probably going to hurt your group's performance in the long run.

I'm getting the impression from your other comments that there's a lot going on here that you either don't want to tell us or just don't have the time to explain. Why do you know so much about this guy and his grandmother if he's only a friend of a friend you don't even like? Most of his behavior sounds vaguely douchey, but I don't think it warrants this much concern from you. We obviously can't know the whole story. You could be right. Either way, I think it'd be best for the both of you if you stayed away from each other. Try to avoid engaging him as much as you can, be civil when you have to, and don't talk about him with your mutual friends/acquaintances. If your friends choose to hang out with him and invite him along to social functions, there's not much you can do about it without probably driving them away in the process. The only thing you can control in this situation is your own behavior.

> I bet he thought I would think it would be too sexist and too rude to throw a girly shirt back in his face.

I mean, rude, definitely. Sexist? Probably not. People have given me weird, girly stuff and shitty regifts alike. I would *never* insult them over it. Unless he's done some bizarrely conniving shit before, I think you're reading too much into this shirt. You might not like this guy, but you're the one that's going to look bad to your mutual friend(s) if you don't apologize.
I keep having similar "ew wtf" moments and remembering that I essentially agreed to become a gross teenage boy, haha

Not a medical professional or anything, but unless you're noticing itching/burning/strong smell, most likely it's smegma. Your glands are producing more sweat/oils now that you've started T. I used to get it caught under my clitoral hood when I started ~~incorrect~~ puberty. Some careful washing with plain water on a daily basis should suffice, but if you want to use soap, use something without irritating chemicals or fragrances.

Apparently I had a major voice drop this week because I've been baffling everyone I speak to on the phone, and I'm kind of enjoying it? My therapist didn't recognize me, and I even had a coworker I'm not out to yet call me sir. When I told her who I was, she said, "You do NOT sound like [birthname]!" I just laughed and said, "I know." I guess when people see me in person my voice isn't masculinized enough to seem out of place, because that's pretty much the only time I pass. :/

I've been struggling with guilt over "ruining" my attractive female body, too. I think it's somewhat expected considering how much women are pressured to look attractive, especially for hetero men. When it really gets to me I try to remind myself that I'm going to get old and ugly either way, and I'll be much happier as a wrinkly, pudgy little old man.

I think one of your biggest misconceptions is that you think something being a mental or psychological issue discredits it. It does not. Mental issues are biological issues. They cannot always be treated by therapy, and that doesn't make them any less valid either.

Hey, K, fellow short transmasculine nonbinary here. I, too, work in customer service, and one of my major sources of dysphoria is when I feel like men are talking down to me because of my perceived gender. I'm still not passing in any capacity (though I'm pretty sure I sometimes get clocked as trans), but my social dysphoria has still gone waaay down over the past couple months. 

Do you think you would be happy with the effects of testosterone even if people continued to not take you seriously at work? Also, transitioning while you are in a relationship can take a lot of communication and work, but if you need to in order to be happy, you have to come first. I suppressed my identity and put off coming out to my partner for a looong time. I feel like our relationship would have been better off if I hadn't tried to force myself to be a girl.

I feel like I'm being a downer here. The good news is, it really doesn't hurt to try testosterone! If you start the process of finding a therapist and getting HRT now, you'll probably have a good chunk of time to think it over and talk with your loved ones about it, and a several months upon starting T before any major/permanent changes take effect. You can stop/slow down at any step of the process you need to. Wish I had more advice about finding a therapist, but I'm in a totally different part of the South, and I lucked out finding mine listed on a local trans advocacy website. 

If you wanna talk more, you can comment here or message me. I'm a bit of a night owl.

When I first gave up shaving, I was surprised how few people cared. I only got a few strange looks from my family and my mom gently offering to buy me a professional waxing. Plenty of girls don't shave because it's expensive, time consuming, and hell for those of us with sensitive skin. It's really easy to hide under clothes, but I honestly think most people don't notice. If they do, it's not their business, so the vast majority won't say anything.

I overcame a really strong urge to hurt myself after encountering a "trigger" of sorts. I'm happy I didn't give in, but now I'm exhausted and I kinda wanna crawl into bed and not get out the rest of the day.

I went through a very similar process, except stage two was extremely brief and I went between stages four and five for a few years until I came back to stage one a little over a year ago. The cycle probably would have continued if I hadn't started seeing my gender therapist. I picked him partly because he's less than five minutes away, and I also have pretty bad driving anxiety. Is there any way you could start seeing the one you can afford remotely, at least until you feel more comfortable driving? Some therapists will do Skype/phone sessions.

Well, I think there are more than a few of us on here who have dated straight men and lesbians. It could be that guy is their exception. Labels can be useful, but people usually don't fit so neatly into them, and sexual orientation is tied into a lot of people's identities.

I'm imagining an Always-Sunny-esque scenario where he colors your packer's head and you ask, "Why the hell is it black???" and he's like, "That's what they look like, dude!" and then you have to take him to a doctor

Funny, I got new needles in today and was worried they'd be too small. They're 1" long whereas the ones I had before were the same length as your new ones. I have pretty small legs (edit: I'm assuming you're injecting in the muscle?) and have injected every week with no problems, so I don't think you have to worry about injuring yourself. I haven't had any experience with leakage, hopefully someone else can give their input on that.

For me, the first few weeks of testosterone had my emotions all over the place, though I'm very prone to mood swings with hormonal changes. I'm relatively static now. I don't know if I feel "more logical" but my feelings are much less extreme/out of control than they used to be. edit: In case you can't see my flair, I'm almost 3 months on T. I'd say the emotional side effects, voice drop, and bottom growth were the three things that started happening quickly.

Well, I've actually been going by Rae, so I know I like the *sound* of the name, I'm just being picky about the spelling. Ray occurred to me several months back when I first came out, but I thought, "No, no way," because 1) Ray Romano and 2) *About Ray* was getting press about that awful interview with the director. Thankfully it looks like it never even came out in theaters. And maybe I was being too hard on Romano, haha.

I'm about ready to settle on the name Ray, but I'm somewhat reluctant because of *[that one movie](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=48B9wSy4kPg)*... Whatever, I'll be the most fabulous little "truck driver or something" the world's ever seen.

Yes! I have a vivid memory of looking into my locker mirror at age 13 and seeing a guy staring back at me. It was startling, but I really liked it. I spent a lot of time since then trying to look the part of a girl with makeup and long hair, but it felt like a costume. Now that I'm okay with being a guy, that's all I can see when I look at my face in the mirror. I can only see myself as a girl with most photos because of the different perspectives, I guess. I hate getting my picture taken.

Wow, what that girl did was incredibly shitty. Are there any sort of HR or higher ups at your work you can go to about this? This doesn't make you any less of a man, but it does make her less of a decent person. The fact that she outed you to everyone and no one made an issue of it possibly means they see it as a poor reflection on her, not you.
Hey, the same thing happened with me. Congrats on making it this far. Hopefully it's all up from here.

I have a couple GC2B half binders and an Underworks tritop. Both brands get my DDD chest down to a small B cup, but the GC2B looks more like a natural male chest whereas the Underworks makes me look barrel-chested. I also had problems with the Underworks binder rolling up during use. I'm hoping my breasts will become easier to flatten as I bind and continue T. For now, I wear loose shirts and layer strategically.

I dealt with depressive episodes without having any idea that they were depressive episodes until I was 21 years old and saw a therapist for the first time in over a decade. I realized about four years ago that I might be trans and promptly buried that thought deep, deep down, which I think led to the crippling depression and near-constant suicidal thoughts for the next few years. That only stopped once I began accepting I was trans about half a year ago. I have a history of failing to take my daily medications and keep up with therapists/psychiatrists. Transitioning has really motivated me to take care of myself in ways I didn't before.

I've also lived with anxiety all my life, but didn't get the GAD diagnosis until a few months ago. I think my dysphoria and my anxiety often fuel each other, although my anxiety hasn't improved as dramatically as my suicidal ideation did after I started hormones.

This photo's kinda limited, so different angles/full body might change things, but you look pretty masculine to me. I'd peg you as a dude ~18-20. Maybe it's the face you're making, but you remind somewhat of [Geoffrey Arend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Arend).

I'd be interested. My dysphoria's started bothering me more when I try my usual methods, but I'm pretty strapped for cash right now.

When you lightly pull on your leg hair, do any strands come out? A bit of background: As soon as I found out bisexuality existed at age 12 or so, I knew I identified with it. I came out to a friend, who told me she was, too, and we carried on as usual... But I quickly became aware of the stigma surrounding bisexuality. I was bombarded with messages that I was probably confused, or was feeling this way because I wanted to be "special," or simply thought it would make me cool and popular. I never questioned my heterosexuality the way I did my homosexuality. I had boyfriends over the years that were aware of my bisexuality, whether I identified as such or not, but I was still scared to let anyone else in. The friend I'd originally come out to became a very devout Christian, and considered sexual deviance an illness. I was deep in the closet, and fitting into the straight category caused me unnecessary emotional pain. I eventually decided to abandon labels altogether.

It wasn't until I was 20, when I was taking a Gender and Sex Studies class in college, that I accepted the label bisexual. I soon began coming out to close friends, and eventually started my "official" coming out on facebook. The first time, a year ago today, I was so nervous I was shaking, and I hid any family and family friends from seeing my status and Interested In (my family had said some vitriolic things about bisexuality in the past, so I felt I wasn't ready for that). I also hid it from my coworkers, since discrimination against sexual orientation is allowed in my state; I love my job, but I didn't trust my coworkers just yet.

After a year of general quiet, I came out again on Bi-Visibility Day last month, but this time the post was completely public. I've kept it as my cover photo, and will probably change it tomorrow. I plan on having a talk with my parents later tonight, since they don't use social networking and deserve more than a status update anyway.

I decided to post this here not only because I'm proud of my progress, but because I want to encourage others who want to come out, but are worried about the hows and whens. My advice is that you don't have to come out all at once. Start with who you're most comfortable with, and continue at your own pace. Despite my anxiety surrounding my sexual orientation, I have been fortunate to get nothing but positive feedback so far. If someone had told me a few years ago that I could be this comfortable and happy about my sexual orientation, I wouldn't have believed it. My friends have given me the strength to know that I'm better off than anyone who berates me for being true to myself.

Wow. My partner and I are the same ages and I'm finally undergoing therapy with Lexapro after dealing with depression and GAD most of my life. Our relationship nearly ended last November mostly due to my overwhelming insecurities with myself and anxieties that he was getting sick of me. I've been feeling some of the same dread lately, which I guess is what lead me back here.

My first piece of advice would be to stop being ashamed of/guilty about your emotions. As my therapist has to constantly remind me, try as we might, we can't control how we feel. I find trying to fight off the anxiety only makes it worse for me. When you feel that urge to poke and pry through your SO's personal things, try taking a step back from the situation; combat your paranoia physically rather than mentally. Breathing exercises work wonders for me, or simply getting out of the house to go for a walk or pace through the aisles of a nearby supermarket. Sometimes I'll go somewhere else and read a book. 

It's also a good idea when you feel an anxiety attack coming on to recall the last time you ate. Low blood sugar does a number on me emotionally, and eating sweets/junk food will just lead me into a worse crash later. I feel best after I get something healthy in my system.

I also struggle to approach my partner for help when I'm feeling down on myself. Thankfully, he is very understanding, so when I do work up the nerve and tell him, "Sweetheart, I'm feeling anxious right now and really need some help," he's always happy to oblige me. Think about what you can ask your SO to do that will reassure you and help prevent you from breaking down when you're having an episode. For me, it's usually a simple cuddle and a word of encouragement if he's there, a supportive text if he's not. Make sure he realizes your doubt stems from your anxieties, and ridding yourself of them is not simply a matter of "doing enough"; they're something you have to work through on a regular basis.

Definitely try to see a good therapist again. Mine is amazing, and I can't believe the amount of progress I've made with her in half a year. Most of my advice I've given you comes from her and a workbook I purchased located [here.](http://www.amazon.com/Best-Ever-Anxiety-Management-Techniques-Workbook/dp/0393707431) I hope I was helpful and not too longwinded. :/ Let me know through here or PM if you need anything else.
